Paragraph:
Translation: Let me see those who have come here to fight, wishing to please the evil-minded son of Dhrtarastra.

Purport: It was an open secret that Duryodhana wanted to usurp the kingdom of the Pandavas by evil plans, in collaboration with his father, Dhrtarastra. Therefore, all persons who had joined the side of Duryodhana must have been birds of the same feather. Arjuna wanted to see them in the battlefield before the fight was begun, just to learn who they were, but he had no intention of proposing peace negotiations with them. It was also a fact that he wanted to see them to make an estimate of the strength which he had to face, although he was quite confident of victory because Krsna was sitting by his side.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Arjuna clarifies his motivation for looking at the enemy. He specifically wants to identify the individuals who have chosen to align themselves with toxicity, injustice, and the 'evil-minded' Duryodhana.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Arjuna draws a firm moral line. He recognizes that those who support an abuser or a toxic leader are complicit in that toxicity ('birds of the same feather'). He sizes up his opposition while maintaining his own confidence.
Outcome/Resolution: He finalizes his threat assessment, mentally categorizing the opposing force not just as an army, but as enablers of adharma.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.confidence: Inner security (rooted in his support system)

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Sanga (Association; understanding that one's character is reflected by the company they keep)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Arjuna views the battlefield through the lens of dharma (righteousness). He identifies the opposing army not merely as combatants, but as individuals who have consciously chosen to support evil. His confidence rests not in his own prowess, but in the presence of the Divine (Krishna) by his side.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This verse showcases a strong, boundaried mindset. Arjuna is mentally preparing to cut ties with toxic individuals. He correctly identifies that enabling bad behavior is a choice, and he evaluates his opposition clearly, shielded from overwhelming anxiety by his secure attachment figure (Krishna).
